items.title: kwb-model has no identity scheme, and every content-addressed thing above it is waiting on one
items.why: The .NET prototype's DeterministicId (SHA-256 into a UUIDv8, with a claim's SourceId deliberately excluded from the hash) is the actual cross-source dedup mechanism: two books asserting the same claim hash to the same id, so a second admission is an upsert rather than a duplicate. D17 and D18 in that prototype's own AGENTS.md are both failures that a stricter identity discipline at the type level would have made harder to reach — a merge that fused two distinct concepts, and a predicate fed into an algorithm that assumed a property it did not have. This item is the decision point for which of those become type-level invariants here rather than review conventions. Measured 2026-09-12 by KWB-9, detail in docs/corpus/prototype-inventory.md: the prototype's identity discipline was implemented once and applied almost nowhere — 87 types in Domain/ default their Id to Guid.NewGuid(), against 9 files that call DeterministicId, and the twelve byte-identical epistemic kernel nodes are all in the first group. DeterministicId.From(params string?[]) is itself the bare static this item's done_when forbids, which is how the discipline became forgettable. Four design details are worth carrying whole and are recorded in the inventory: the version-8 UUID tag rather than an impersonated v5, the 0x1F separator chosen because whitespace normalisation cannot produce it, case deliberately not normalised, and a null part kept distinct from an absent one. D20 belongs here too: the prototype declares `public double Confidence { get; set; } = 1.0` in 40 Domain types (41 counting one init), so an unset confidence reads as certain — the unfinished half of that prototype's own ADR 0001 follow-up, whose value objects (Confidence, RigorLevel, AccessibilityLevel) sit in Domain/Values alongside the 40 bare doubles.
items.done_when: kwb-model exposes a content-derived identity type whose construction requires the bytes it is derived from (no bare `new` that accepts an arbitrary string), documents which fields participate in the hash and why, and has tests demonstrating that two inputs differing only in an explicitly-excluded field (the source) produce the same identity.

items.title: The universal epistemic type kernel is named in every document about this product and designed in none of them
items.why: The .NET prototype's Domain/Universal — a discipline-neutral type and relation hierarchy that domain-specific YAML packs specialize — is the piece the prototype's own architecture treats as most load-bearing. Porting its type *tree* (the ~30 hardcoded UniversalType entries) without re-deriving why its relation kinds are the closed set would be porting the easy half and leaving the actual design decision unmade here. CORRECTED 2026-09-12 by KWB-9, measured in docs/corpus/prototype-inventory.md: this item previously said 'nine relation kinds'. UniversalRelationKind has 21 members — nine cross-domain discovery discriminations plus twelve structural families (Taxonomic, Compositional, Dependency, Logical, Evidential, Normative, Representational, Functional, Temporal, Contextual, Contradiction, Contrast). An implementer who re-derives only the nine re-derives the vocabulary of discovery and inherits unexamined the vocabulary that types every relation the packs actually declare. Three further measurements bear on this item. First, the prototype's real answer to D18 is not the nine kinds but UniversalRelationKindExtensions.Constraint() — a per-kind algebra commitment checked by AlgebraViolations on the pack-load path (DomainPackValidator.cs:196 from DomainPackRegistry.cs:86) — and that is Exercised, whereas the node types are only Declared and Implemented per D-003. Second, twelve types implementing IEpistemicNode are byte-identical apart from the type name, and six of them reach no consumer at all, so they are one hypothesis expressed twelve times rather than twelve concepts. Third, nine hand-written IDomainModule implementations (1,430 lines) have zero consumers outside their own directory and are kept in sync with the YAML packs by a drift test that is their only reader — do not rebuild the twin. Of a pack's seven declared contributions only the relation algebra reaches the runtime, and ValidationConstraint carries a prose Description with no predicate, so no pack validation constraint can fire.
items.done_when: kwb-domain states, as a record, what a UniversalType hierarchy must guarantee (closed under IsA, one KnowledgeLayer per type) and what the relation vocabulary must guarantee — for all 21 kinds, not only the nine discovery discriminations: that they are complete and mutually exclusive, or a documented reason they are not, and what algebra each kind commits its specializations to — before any domain pack format is designed against it.

items.title: kwb-retrieval and kwb-mcp have no query surface, and the prototype's mutation-exclusion decision (its own D10) is not yet a property of this workspace's types
items.why: The prototype's MCP host exposes nine read-only tools with every reply bounded so an agent cannot exhaust its own context, and excludes mutation from that surface entirely. Read this as a contract worth preserving independent of the protocol carrying it: the type an MCP tool handler is built against should not have a mutating method to call by mistake. The nine tools are confirmed by measurement (search, get_concept, neighbours, path, proofs_for, claims_for, code_for, gaps_in_source, list_connection_hypotheses). KWB-9 attaches a second incident to this item, detailed in docs/corpus/prototype-incidents.md as D19-B: the prototype's AGENTS.md carries two distinct incidents both numbered D19, and the second one — 'a filter that applies itself is a check nobody asked for' — is the one its own ROADMAP does not carry forward. Its subject is which world a read returns. A global query filter rewrote every query including ones written by people who had never heard of it, so merge-audit resolved none of the merge log's ids against the current view, printed 'nothing has been merged away' and exited 0 — every merge on record could have been wrong and the gate would have passed. No filter at all failed the other way. The prototype's answer is two interfaces (IConceptRepository current, IConceptHistory every version) so that needing retired rows is a dependency visible in a constructor, liveness is one expression rather than three hand-written copies, and an audit carries an independent expectation and throws rather than reporting a zero. That is the same structural discipline this item already states for mutation, applied to temporality; two read types, not one type with a flag. A second observation, measured against nomos 2026-09-12 and detailed in docs/corpus/nomos-as-precedent.md, bears on the second half of this item: nomos-mcp holds a tool CATALOGUE and no protocol. Its ServedTool names which tools exist, the sentence each publishes and the schema each accepts, while the whole initialize/tools-list/tools-call/ping handshake, notification suppression and framing come from xvpe-remote-call-backend-json — its own band entry states the test that the split was drawn correctly, that 'this crate names no protocol library at all'. The prototype's nine tools are a catalogue in exactly that sense. Whether this repository may take that edge is KWB-8's question, not this item's; what this item can take from it either way is that the protocol is not the part worth owning, and read-only-ness is.

items.title: This repository has a work/ledger.json and no tool that operates on it
items.why: AGENTS.md documents claim, finish, and territory as this repository's coordination mechanism, but nomos-ledger — the crate that actually implements those verbs in f:/repos/nomos — is Nomos-specific by location, not by semantics; ARC-ECOSYSTEM-001 already names it a candidate whose subject does not require the thing being coordinated to be software. D-135's new default-to-XVPE policy for genuinely domain-neutral code makes this the first real test of that policy in practice, not a hypothetical. The absence now has a concrete victim: KWB-9 ran to completion and could not be finished through the ledger, because AGENTS.md forbids hand-editing an item to Done and no tool exists to transition it any other way. It is therefore parked in Claimed with its artifacts delivered — which is exactly the state this item exists to stop being the only available one. Measured against nomos 2026-09-12, detail in docs/corpus/nomos-as-precedent.md: this decision has a cheaper fourth option than the three named above, and a different governing record than the one named below. The fourth option is to adopt nomos-ledger's SCHEMA without adopting any dependency. Running nomos's own binary against this board — `nomos work validate` from this repository's root — reads this file, parses it, and refuses it at exit 5 with `missing field kind`. Field by field the two schemas are one: Territory is identical (resolution/paths/patterns), ItemState already includes Claimed, and abandoned/displaced/declined are already here. The entire gap is two closed-set fields (kind: capability|decision|validation|correction|cleanup, origin: required|proposed) and schema_version 1 against nomos's 5. Both containers use serde(deny_unknown_fields) per OD-LEDGER-008, which is why the refusal is total rather than partial. On the governing record: D-135 decides where NEW domain-neutral code is authored and is explicit that it does not weaken the proof requirement for code moving after the fact, so evaluating D-135's admission test against nomos-ledger evaluates the wrong test — nomos-ledger is 14,008 lines of existing code, and the clause that governs moving it is D-122 as adopted into ARC-ECOSYSTEM-001: two products demonstrating materially identical domain-neutral semantics. This board being nomos's schema minus two fields is close to that proof and is materially stronger than the hypothetical D-122 exists to refuse. Two bounds: XVPE has no work-ledger crate today (xvpe-frame-ledger is timing, xvpe-task-* is runtime concurrency), and nomos already measured Territory as a migration candidate and rejected it under OD-PLATFORM-003's criterion — no XVPE site was found doing it worse. That criterion asks what XVPE is missing and is silent on what a second product needs, which is this item's actual question. Finally, the mechanism this repository most concretely lacks is the lease: nomos's claim lapses, `list` reports it lapsed rather than claimed, and Take_Over recovers it while preserving the displaced claim. KWB-9 being unfinishable is that absence, measured. CLAIM NOTE, moved here by KWB-13 because nomos-ledger's Claim carries holder and timestamps only: Claimed 2026-09-12, territory narrowed from [docs/records, work] to [docs/records] on release: `work` was needed only to claim this item and to add KWB-13, and holding it afterwards blocked KWB-13 — the item that finishes this one. That is OD-LEDGER-001's authoring mistake, made for the second time in one session on this board, which is itself evidence for what D-005 decided. Decision recorded as D-005: adopt nomos-ledger's schema, use its binary as the interim tool, and defer ownership. The three options this item named are all about owning ledger code; measurement showed the question was wrong-shaped, and the two options it did not name are the ones that answer it. KWB-13 is the follow-on the decision implies. Parked in Claimed rather than Done for the same reason KWB-9 is: no tool exists to transition it, which is this item's own subject. KWB-13 landing is what makes both transitionable.

items.title: The XVPE dependency hazard rests on a compile failure that no longer reproduces, and a stale premise is not permission to take the dependency
items.why: AGENTS.md refuses a path dependency on f:/repos/xvpe because its foundations tier does not compile, citing xvpe-dataflow at 62 errors as of the last check from the Nomos side. Measured 2026-09-12 from the xvpe workspace, `cargo check -p <crate>` exits 0 for xvpe-primitives, xvpe-serialization, xvpe-sync-primitives, xvpe-collections, xvpe-algorithms, xvpe-dataflow, xvpe-math, xvpe-formula and xvpe-json-text — xvpe-dataflow itself finishing with 106 warnings and no errors. That measurement covers libraries only: no tests, no --all-targets, and no doctests, which `check` never compiles. So the hazard's stated premise no longer reproduces, and that says nothing about whether the position it supports is still right: Nomos's own D-130 may rest on reasons the compile failure never carried, and a build observation is not an architecture decision. The failure this item exists to prevent is someone reading a green `cargo check` as permission. The observation this item carries — that the premise is stale — is settled, and measurement against nomos on 2026-09-12 found it stale a SECOND way, which the compile-check never touched. Detail in docs/corpus/nomos-as-precedent.md. AGENTS.md and README.md here both refuse the dependency 'for the same reason Nomos's own D-130 gives', and OD-PLATFORM-003 retired that clause for this crossing: 'No, for the XVPE crossing. Nomos is built on top of XVPE. XVPE is the engine. This workspace is an application over it, in the same sense the knowledge workbench is.' That record characterises THIS repository's relationship to XVPE, not only its own. It closes exactly one crossing and names it — nomos may not reach a `kwb-` prefix, enforced by Test_No_Crate_May_Name_The_Sibling_Knowledge_Workbench with an empty allowlist — and that direction is nomos to kwb. Nothing found in nomos's record set closes kwb to xvpe; a reader who takes 'the KWB crossing is still closed' as bearing on this item has read the direction backwards. Complicating rather than settling it: D-130 itself still reads status accepted, version 2, and still says adoption is by git reference and commit SHA into one quarantined crate and is 'never a path dependency', while nomos's own AGENTS.md records six crates naming xvpe by relative path and ten reaching one transitively. OD-PLATFORM-003's relations target AGT-006 and not D-130, and ARC-CONNECTOR-001 still says 'D-130 is untouched'. That divergence is nomos's to resolve; what belongs here is that this repository is citing the side of it that practice left behind. Mechanically the option is costed: kwb, nomos and xvpe are siblings under /f/repos, nomos spells its edges path = '../../../../xvpe/crates/...', and cargo metadata --no-deps on nomos exits 0, so the same spelling resolves from here — at the cost OD-PLATFORM-003 accepted deliberately, that the workspace stops building without the sibling checkout present and fails at manifest resolution in a way that reads nothing like the real cause. items.title: Steps 7 and 8 of the product loop are what make it a loop, and nothing in the prototype or on this board owns either
items.why: The design corpus states KWB's central product loop in ten steps (topic 054 in the game plan): a passage is ingested, claims are extracted, claims are connected to normalized concepts, relation assertions are proposed, evidence and context are attached, existing assertions are corroborated or challenged, derived connections are recomputed, stale syntheses are invalidated, users inspect why a connection exists, and users compare current and historical interpretations. Measured against the prototype 2026-09-12, detail in docs/corpus/what-kwb-is-for.md: steps 1-4 and 6 are substantially built, and steps 7 and 8 are not partial but zero. `DerivationDependency` 0 files, `Staleness` 0 files, `Invalidate` 0 files, `GraphVersion` 0 files. DerivationLedger looks like it should cover them and does not: DerivationRecord is {RunId, ChunkId, NodeId, ModelVersion, PromptHash, ResponseHash, Rationale, Outcome}, which records that a node came from a chunk via a model. That is a provenance record, not a dependency edge — nothing anywhere says this synthesis depends on these claims, so a changed claim invalidates it. Without recompute-and-invalidate, steps 1-6 are a pipeline that runs once rather than a loop, which is the prototype's actual condition: it compiled a corpus and then had no mechanism to notice the corpus changing underneath it. Four independent readings land here. The nine operations (415) put `revise` among the absent. The prototype's own ROADMAP lists thirteen gaps verified absent from its source tree and `DerivationDependency` and staleness propagation are first. The corpus's own sequencing (topic 053) makes 'add derivation dependencies and staleness' its Phase 3. items.title: kwb-model can derive an identity from normalized text and from nothing else, so the document store cannot address a document without either losing bytes or minting identity twice
items.why: KWB-2 is the first consumer of KWB-1 and does not fit through it. Derivation offers With_Text, With_Identity and With_Absent; With_Text runs Normalize, which collapses every whitespace run and strips every C0/C1 control character. That is exactly right for a claim, where a reflow is not an edit, and it is destructive for a stored document. Two documents differing only in indentation derive one identity, so the second write finds the first already present, reports success, and the second document bytes are gone. That is a D17 incident in the precise shape D17 names: a write that reports success while destroying evidence it had no basis to destroy. The alternative open to kwb-store inside its own territory is to hash bytes itself with sha2, which AGENTS.md refuses as introducing a second authority for something already governed, and which would put two derivation layouts in one workspace with nothing asserting they agree. So identity for opaque bytes is kwb-model work, discovered by KWB-2, and it is a door on the existing Derivation rather than a new scheme.
items.done_when: Derivation admits raw bytes as a participating field through one door that does not normalize them, documented where it is defined with what it does not do and why a caller must not reach for it when the field is text. The layout keeps every property KWB-1 paid for: the field name participates, the separator still cannot be forged from inside a value, and an absent field still occupies its place. Tests assert that two byte strings differing only in whitespace derive different identities, that a byte field and a text field of the same name and content do not collide, and that a value containing the separator byte cannot forge a field boundary through the bytes door. kwb-model builds and tests green, and no caller outside kwb-model is required for this item to close.

items.title: This repository has no .gitattributes, two files checked in with CRLF and the rest with LF, and a gate that will one day compare bytes
items.why: core.autocrlf is true and .gitattributes is absent, so what lands in a working tree depends on the machine that checked it out. Measured today: kwb-model content_identity.rs and tests.rs are CRLF on disk, every other source file is LF, and committing anything prints a warning per file about endings changing the next time git touches it. git diff reports none of this, because git compares normalized content, so the disagreement is invisible to exactly the tool a session would reach for. The cost is not hypothetical in a repository built this way. A gate that compares raw bytes -- a generated table, a golden file, a digest of a source tree -- fails against a checkout git calls clean, and the session that inherits it has no way to see why. This repository already derives identity from bytes, so it is more exposed to this than most.
items.done_when: A .gitattributes at the repository root declares text handling explicitly rather than leaving it to a per-machine setting, the two CRLF files are normalized so the tree is internally consistent, and the whole workspace still builds, tests and lints green afterwards. A line-ending change that silently altered a source file would be the failure this item exists to prevent, so the verification is the workspace test run and not an inspection of the diff.

items.title: The board cannot reserve a record that has not been numbered yet, so every decision item reserves the whole records directory and the board serialises
items.why: Measured across one session that closed six items. Adding an item to correct D-004 -- a correction D-004 itself mandates -- was refused because docs/records is reserved by KWB-3, which nobody is holding. Five of the items authored with a record in their done_when reserve the directory rather than a file, and add refuses any new item overlapping an open one, so while any decision item is unclosed no new decision item can be proposed at all. The refusal suggests retiring the blocking item, which inverts the situation. This is not carelessness in the authoring. The tool supports file granularity and says so, but only for a record that already exists: --amends reserves a published file, and there is no way to reserve a record identifier that has not been allocated yet. An item that will write a decision cannot name what it will write, so the only reservation available to it is the directory. That is the root cause, and it is a gap in the mechanism rather than in the items. Three smaller findings sit beside it and are cheap to state: work show advertises an item in full and prints no why, no done_when and no territory, so a session following the loop must parse work/ledger.json by hand to see the predicate it is told to run; --amends refuses the identifier a record declares for itself and accepts only the path, though the identifier is how every record in this repository cites every other; and the board reserves ground without defending it, which cost two territory slips in this session alone, both the same shape of writing first and reserving after.
items.done_when: An observation document records each finding with what was measured and the command that showed it, separates the root cause from its symptoms, and says for each whether the remedy belongs to how items are authored here or to the ledger tool this repository borrowed and took no dependency on under D-005. Where the remedy is the tool, the document states what the mechanism would have to offer rather than proposing an implementation, because that code is not this repository. It closes no finding by itself and asserts nothing about nomos, which is a sibling this repository does not govern.

items.title: D-008 said the second store decision was blocked on the domain types, and KWB-3 and KWB-4 have closed
items.why: D-008 measured that the bands table names one store where the prototype evidence describes two: an immutable artifact store, which kwb-store is, and a mutable versioned graph, which nothing here has and no row names. Seven of the eight storage requirements the prototype proved -- one liveness expression, uniqueness under it, which-world reads, temporal reconstruction, contradiction refusal, the lease, ranked retrieval -- land on the second, and kwb-domain names the types without saying where they live. D-008 deliberately stopped at naming the gap and recorded that deciding it was blocked on what those types are, which is KWB-3 and KWB-4. Both have now closed, so the blocker has cleared and the decision is owed. It is also blocking work already on the board: KWB-6 requires that current-version and all-versions reads be distinct types rather than one type with a flag, which is D19-B translated into this workspace, and over a content-addressed store where every document is immutable and there is exactly one version of everything that distinction is two names for identical behaviour. Building it now would produce a gate that passes because there is nothing for it to catch, which is the defect rather than the requirement. Durability is the other half: kwb-store holds documents in memory for the length of a process, recorded by KWB-2 as a deferral to this question and not an oversight.

It answers against D-008s eight requirements explicitly, requirement by requirement, saying which the decision meets, which it defers and which it declines, because a storage decision that does not say that is a decision nobody can check. It names no database and no library, and where it defers it names what would settle the deferral. D-008s warning attaches: the cost of a retrieval shape is invisible to correctness tests, measured at 38 ms against 1.3 ms on byte-identical rows, so a choice made here cannot be validated by the tests passing.

items.title: D-005 deferred owning ledger code because one product used it, and KWB using it makes two
items.why: D-005 decided this repository adopts nomos-ledger schema and takes no dependency on its code, and its reasoning was explicit about why: D-135 governs where new domain-neutral code is authored, nomos-ledger is 14,008 existing lines, so ARC-ECOSYSTEM-001 two-product proof governs instead, and at the time there was one product. There are now two. This repository operates its board by running that binary daily, so the condition D-005 named as deciding the question has been met by events rather than by argument. OD-LEDGER-001 measured what the current arrangement costs: an item cannot reserve a record it has not numbered, so every decision item reserves the whole records directory, and while any decision item is open no new decision item can be proposed at all. That is not a grievance about a tool, it is the predictable result of a shared mechanism having no owner who can change it -- this repository cannot fix it because D-005 correctly says the code is not ours, and Nomos has no reason to prioritise a constraint it does not feel. A work ledger is not knowledge and it is not software-engineering analysis. It is a coordination mechanism, which is exactly the shape D-135 and ARC-ECOSYSTEM-001 assign to XVPE, and xvpe-event-journal is the worked precedent: it came out of the reference miner because the part that does not know what is being journalled was trapped where nothing else could reach it.
items.done_when: A record here states this repository position -- that the work ledger is a shared coordination mechanism and belongs to XVPE under D-135, that D-005 deferral condition has been met, and what this repository would consume and what it would keep. It does not decide the ecosystem question, because AGENTS.md routes that to ARC-ECOSYSTEM-001 in Nomos and this repository does not restate what it does not own; it states a position and names the evidence, so the upstream decision has something measured to act on. It proposes no crate name and moves no code.

items.title: D-010 decided a scope belongs to an assertion and there is no assertion type, so claims currently have nowhere to put a source or a scope
items.why: KWB-4 built Claim and Concept, and both deliberately exclude the source and the scope from their identity -- the source so two references asserting one claim become one claim with two citations, the scope because D-010 measured that a scope in the identity would make a benchmark and a mere preference saying the same thing two rows that can never learn of each other. Both exclusions are right and both leave a hole. A claim currently records what is asserted and nothing about who asserted it, from where, or over what domain, so the citations the whole dedup mechanism exists to accumulate have nowhere to accumulate. D-010 named the missing type in as many words and said it is where a grade attaches. D-004 version 2 puts both halves of it on closed ground: the verification and provenance axis of the evidence model closed on measurement, and what a scope belongs to closed by D-010 needing no miner input at all. What stays open is the grading, which is the epistemic-strength model and is pending rather than stranded.
items.done_when: kwb-domain has an assertion type that binds a claim to the source asserting it and the scope it is asserted at, with an identity derived from all three -- so that one claim carries many assertions and two assertions of one claim by two sources are two rows that meet at the claim. It carries no confidence, grade or strength of any kind, and a test fixes that absence, because the epistemic-strength model is on D-004 held list as pending and an assertion that graded itself now would be the settable Confidence = 1.0 the prototype shipped in forty types. Tests defend the properties rather than the accessors: two sources asserting one claim produce one claim and two assertions, the same source asserting the same claim twice is one assertion, and a scope change produces a different assertion of the same claim.

items.title: Admission hands back concepts and claims, the graph holds concepts, and nothing connects them
items.why: KWB-5 built the pipeline and KWB-24 built versioned state, and between them there is nothing. Admit returns its concepts and claims to its caller deliberately -- D19 forbids enqueueing for a consumer that does not exist, and at the time D-008 had measured that the store claims belong in had no crate. D-012 answered that and KWB-24 built it, so the consumer now exists and the deliberate gap has become an ordinary one. Left as it is, this repository has an ingestion pipeline whose output reaches nothing and a graph nothing fills: complete, tested code connected to no other code, which is the defect this family of repositories produces most often. The graph is also concept-only. Claims and assertions are versioned by the same mechanism or they are not versioned at all, and a claim that cannot be closed cannot be corrected -- while a concept can. That asymmetry is not a decision anybody made.
items.done_when: Admission writes its concepts and claims into versioned state through one call, and returns the new graph value rather than mutating one -- so the caller still holds what it had, which is what makes the previous version a thing that was kept. The graph holds claims and assertions as well as concepts, under one liveness rule and still with exactly one definition of it. Tests defend the connection rather than the pieces: what admission reports as admitted is what the resulting graph holds, a re-admitted source adds no duplicate concept, and a claim whose concept is closed is reachable through the all-versions read and not through the current one -- because a claim about a retired concept is not a current claim, and saying so is the point of having one liveness rule rather than two.

items.title: Nothing can close a concept, so a merge loser is a state only a test has ever produced, and a supersede records no evidence authorising it
items.why: Two findings from the same sweep that found KWB-36. Standing has three variants and production constructs only Asserted -- Retired and Superseded appear solely in the encode and decode halves of replay, which means the closing path can only ever read records nothing writes. Merge_Losers, the question D19-B says merge-audit needed and asked of the wrong world, can therefore only ever answer about an empty set, and the whole current-versus-historical distinction this repository has spent several records justifying has nothing to distinguish. And the second, which is the sharper one: Standing::Superseded carries its successor and nothing else. D17 is that destruction requires evidence, and the question it demands be answerable before a delete, deprecate, supersede or overwrite is "what belief authorises this, and what would falsify it". A supersede that records the successor and not the reason cannot answer it. The prototype was better here -- it kept a ConceptMerge log its own merge-audit re-read -- and this repository, which cites that incident in four records, currently has no place to put the answer.
items.done_when: Closing a concept records what authorised it. A supersede names its successor and the belief behind it, a retirement names its reason, and neither is constructible without one -- so the question D17 demands be answerable is answerable by construction rather than by whoever remembers to write it down. The reason survives a record and a replay. The command line can retire and supersede, so the closing path is reachable outside a test and a merge loser is a state the product can actually produce. Superseding something into itself is refused, and so is superseding into a concept the graph does not hold, because both are merges whose successor cannot be resolved and D17 is about not destroying on a belief nobody checked.

items.why: The surveys are measurements of the prototype and cannot go stale, but each incident ends with a What would encode it here section, and those are prescriptions about code that did not exist when they were written and does now. items.title: Admission takes a list of extractions rather than an extractor, so the seam the admission rule requires does not exist
items.why: The README first line says KWB ingests references and builds a graph of the concepts they teach. It cannot: nothing reads a document and decides what it says, and a person types the claims through --says. The obvious next step is an extractor, and the corpus own admission rule says where it may not go. Its second test is whether a feature would still make sense if the model were replaced by a perfect human annotator -- yes means it is KWB, no means it is an AI capability KWB happens to use. Extraction as a step passes that test, because a person reading a passage and writing down what it asserts is a real step. Extraction by a model fails it. So the step belongs here and the model-backed implementation does not, and building one inside kwb-ingest would put an AI capability inside the knowledge engine, which is the one thing the rule exists to prevent. There is a second reason to do this before any extractor exists rather than after. kwb admit --says is already an implementation of that port -- it is literally the perfect human annotator the rule describes -- and it is unnamed, so the seam is being used without being declared. Declaring it costs almost nothing now and is a refactor of every caller later.

items.title: Whether a reading's location and protocol belong on the assertion, when corroboration is counted by assertions
items.why: KWB-47 declared a contract carrying where in a source something was read and under what protocol, and KWB-53 established that admission discards both -- so the invariant that every admitted claim identifies its source occurrence and extraction protocol is unmet, and there is no record of the decision that would settle how. The obvious move is to put them on the Assertion, and it is the wrong one in a way that is only visible once corroboration is counted: this repository counts corroboration by assertions. The test that exercises the mechanism every identity decision here was made to support says so -- two different documents, the same claim text, one claim and two assertions, each naming the address of the document it was read out of. If lineage entered an assertion's identity, re-reading one book under a new prompt would produce a second assertion for the same claim from the same source, and the count that says two sources agree would say two when one source was read twice. That is the reference miner's measured failure reached from the other direction: its claim identity absorbs the source path and page window, so two sources' assertions can never meet. And carrying them without identifying by them is the other failure, KWB-32's: two readings meeting at one assertion that holds one of their lineages is a value disagreeing with itself.
items.done_when: A record decides where a reading's location and protocol live and what may never absorb them, with the corroboration-count argument as its measurement rather than as a preference. It states the consequence of each rejected placement in terms of something this repository already measured. If the answer is that provenance about a reading is its own thing rather than a field on an existing one, the record says what that costs, what it does not decide, and the condition that settles the rest -- the shape D-012 and D-014 use, where a decision names the consumer whose absence defers the build. It does not build it: nothing here reads a source yet, every reading is a person through Stated, and a mechanism built before its consumer is what D-009 and the queue in D19 are both about. Relations are declared so the contract test finds them from both ends.

Nothing in this repository reads a source -- KWB-47 declared the extraction contract and its only implementation is Stated, a person typing through --says, so what the graph holds is what a person said a reference asserts and not what the reference teaches. items.title: The eaten-continuation scanner reads Rust only, and the fifth instance landed in the one command a reader is told to type
items.why: KWB-52 built a scanner for a literal whose line continuation was eaten by a scripted edit, and it reads .rs files under crates/. KWB-56 found the fifth instance outside that reach: both kwb admit lines in README.md's Trying it section carried seven spaces before --says, in the only command a new reader is asked to run. The scanner would never have seen it. The damage is a property of an edit, not of a language -- anything a scripted edit writes can lose a continuation, and a console block is the worst place for it to land because a reader copies it. Markdown is not Rust, so the Rust rule does not transfer: indentation is meaningful in markdown, tables are aligned deliberately, and a fenced block holds text whose layout is its content. A scan that flagged those would be turned off, which is the failure mode KWB-52's own exemptions were written against.
items.done_when: A guard fails on a run of spaces in the middle of a command line inside a fenced console block anywhere under docs/ and in README.md and AGENTS.md. It reads only the command lines of console fences, because that is where the damage lands and where a reader copies from, and it says why it does not scan markdown generally -- deliberate alignment, meaningful indentation, and fenced content whose layout is the point. Each exemption is demonstrated by a real shape from these files rather than described. It is shown to detect the instance KWB-56 fixed, reconstructed, and the reader is asserted to have found the files and the fences, because a scanner that reads nothing passes everywhere. If it flags anything else in the tree, that is a finding and is fixed rather than exempted.
